n: Eliphaz begins the third and final round of speeches. Now he openly accuses Job of specific sins — none of which are true.
Eliphaz asks whether a person’s goodness benefits God at all. A wise man helps himself, but God doesn’t need anything from us.
Does it give God any pleasure or gain if Job is righteous? Eliphaz pictures God as distant and unaffected — a view the rest of scripture corrects.

f.w: Is it any pleasure to the Almighty

n: Eliphaz asks whether God is punishing Job because Job is so pious. Obviously not, he implies — so it must be for sin.

f.g: Because of your reverence — because you are devout.

n: Now the open charge: “Isn’t your wickedness great and your sins endless?” Eliphaz has decided Job must be guilty.

f.g: Your sins without end — a charge the narrator has already refuted (1:1, 8).

n: He invents crimes: taking collateral from relatives without cause and stripping poor people of their clothes.

f.g: Taking a garment or item as security for a loan; the law limited this to protect the poor.

n: He accuses Job of refusing water to the tired and bread to the hungry — the opposite of the generosity Job describes in chapters 29 and 31.
Eliphaz suggests Job used his power and status to take the land for himself and the privileged few.

f.g: Literally “the man of arm” — a powerful person who takes what he wants.

n: He claims Job sent widows away empty and crushed orphans. Job will answer this directly in 29:12-13 and 31:16-21.

f.g: Orphans — those most vulnerable in ancient society.

n: That, Eliphaz concludes, explains Job’s traps and sudden terrors.
Darkness blinds him and floods overwhelm him — images of total calamity.

f.g: Flood waters — a common image for overwhelming trouble.

n: Eliphaz points to God’s height above the stars to stress how great God is.
He accuses Job of thinking that God is too far away to know or judge what happens below.
He puts words in Job’s mouth: “Thick clouds hide him, so he can’t see as he walks the dome of the sky.” Job never said this.

f.g: The vault or dome of the sky.

n: Eliphaz asks if Job will follow the ancient path of the wicked.

f.g: The well-worn path of past sinners.

n: Those wicked were snatched away before their time, their foundations washed away — perhaps a memory of Noah’s Flood.
They told God to leave them alone and asked what the Almighty could do to them.
Yet God had filled their homes with good things. Eliphaz then repeats Job’s own words from 21:16, “the counsel of the wicked is far from me,” perhaps mocking him.

f.w: the counsel of the wicked is far from me

n: The righteous rejoice and the innocent laugh when the wicked fall.

f.w: The righteous see it, and are glad

n: They say, “Our enemies are destroyed, and fire has eaten up what they left.”
Eliphaz turns to an appeal: make peace with God and good will come. The advice is sound in itself, even if his assumptions about Job are wrong.

f.g: Come to know God; be reconciled to him.

n: Accept God’s instruction and store his words in your heart.

f.w: lay up his words in thine heart

n: If Job returns to God and removes sin from his household, he will be restored.
Eliphaz promises riches — gold as plentiful as dust and Ophir’s fine gold as common as river stones.

f.g: Ophir was a far-off land famous for fine gold.

n: God himself will be Job’s treasure and his precious silver.

f.g: Better “your gold” — God himself will be Job’s true wealth.

n: Then Job will delight in God and look up to him with confidence instead of shame.

f.w: lift up thy face unto God

n: His prayers will be heard and he will fulfill the vows he made.

f.g: Fulfill promises made to God, often with a thank offering.

n: Whatever he decides will succeed, and light will shine on his path.

f.w: the light shall shine upon thy ways

n: When others are brought low, Job will be able to say “Lift up!” and God will save the humble.

f.w: he shall save the humble person

n: God will deliver even the guilty because of Job’s clean hands. Ironically, this is exactly what happens: God accepts Job’s prayer for Eliphaz himself (42:8).

f.g: Better “even one who is not innocent.”
